oneSentence: A broadly trained machine-learning model can be adapted for many different tasks without starting training again from nothing.
plainExplanation:
A foundation model is a machine-learning model trained first on a very large and varied collection of data. That first stage is often called pretraining. The aim is to build a general starting point that can later be adapted to many tasks.

What goes in at the start is usually large-scale data, such as text, images, audio or a mix of these. During training, the system adjusts many numerical settings, often called parameters, so that it becomes better at predicting patterns in that data. What comes out is not a finished service by itself, but a reusable base that others can fine-tune, instruct, connect to tools or place inside an application.

This is different from a model built for just one narrow job, such as detecting a specific defect in one factory or forecasting one type of demand. A foundation model is intended to be general-purpose within the kinds of data it was trained on. It may support summarising, classification, drafting, search assistance or other tasks after adaptation, but that does not mean it is equally good or safe for all of them.

People often confuse foundation models with large language models. Many large language models are foundation models, but not all foundation models work only with language. Some handle images, speech or several data types together. The exact boundary is still debated, so the term is useful but not perfectly settled.

everydayAnalogy.title: A well-organised library as a starting point
everydayAnalogy.story: A city library receives millions of books in many languages and spends years cataloguing them by subject, author, date and keywords. Later, different readers use that same catalogue for different goals: one person finds climate reports, another builds a reading list for children, and a third locates books on public health in French. The catalogue was not built for only one question, but it helps many later tasks start quickly. Staff still need to check whether a search result is relevant, current and appropriate for the reader.

mapping.analogyElement: the large catalogue built from many books

many downstream tasks such as summarising, classifying or searching

mapping.analogyElement: the same catalogue reused instead of rebuilt each time
mapping.aiElement: a base model adapted rather than training a new model from scratch
human oversight, evaluation and task-specific safeguards

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A library catalogue is a human-made index with explicit entries. A foundation model does not store knowledge in neat labelled cards. It learns statistical patterns through numerical adjustment, and it can generate fluent but wrong output. Also, a catalogue mostly helps you find existing books, while a foundation model can also produce new text, images or other outputs.

visual.title: How a foundation model becomes useful for many tasks

From that single model, three branches lead to different adapted uses such as summarising, image labelling and search assistance. Read from left to right, then down the branches.

visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a left-to-right flow. First, a box labelled 'Large datasets' shows that training begins with broad data such as text, images and audio. An arrow leads to 'Pretraining', where the model learns statistical patterns by adjusting parameters. Another arrow leads to a central box labelled 'Foundation model or base model', showing the reusable result of that first training stage. From there, three arrows branch outward to 'summarise documents', 'classify images' and 'search assistant'. The main message is that one broadly pretrained model can be adapted for several different tasks instead of training a separate model from zero for each task.

workedExample.scenario: A research team builds a document assistant for environmental reports in English, Arabic and French.
workedExample.input: A pretrained multilingual text model and 50,000 approved public documents, plus 2,000 human-reviewed examples of good summaries.
process: The team starts with a broadly pretrained language model rather than training a new one from zero.
They adapt it using the reviewed examples so it learns the organisation's preferred summary format and terminology.
They test it on 300 unseen documents and compare its summaries with human ratings for accuracy, omission and clarity.
They deploy it only for first-draft summaries, with a human reviewer required before any text is shared.
workedExample.result: The same base model can now produce draft summaries, suggest keywords and help retrieval across several languages, but each use still needs separate evaluation and oversight.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN office wants an internal search tool over policy guidance, training materials and publicly shareable reference documents used by staff in different duty stations.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: A foundation model can serve as the starting component for multilingual search and question-answering across many document types, reducing the need to build a separate model for each narrow task.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload confidential, personal, protection-sensitive, security-sensitive or operational information into an unapproved public AI service; use approved systems, limit the data and keep human review over outputs.

whyItMatters: Non-specialists hear this term in procurement, governance and risk discussions because it changes how AI systems are built and bought. Instead of commissioning a separate model for each use, organisations may start from one broadly trained model and adapt it. That can reduce time and cost, but it also changes the questions leaders should ask: what data was used in pretraining, what limits are known, what tasks has it actually been evaluated for, who controls the weights or access, and what safeguards exist for privacy, bias, safety and accountability. The label also matters because not every impressive model is a suitable foundation for public-sector work.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A foundation model can do any task well straight away.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Broad pretraining gives a useful starting point, not guaranteed competence. Performance varies by task, language, domain and context. A model may need further adaptation, testing and safeguards before it is reliable enough for real use.

Many chatbots are built on foundation models, but the terms are not the same. A chatbot is an application or interface. A foundation model is the underlying broadly pretrained model, which may support chat, search, image tasks or other uses.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a model is called foundational, its output is authoritative.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The term describes how the model was trained and reused, not whether each answer is correct. Outputs still need verification because models can reflect gaps in data, produce errors and perform unevenly across topics or languages.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is a large starter model trained on broad data so people can adapt it for many different jobs later.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: A foundation model is a machine-learning model, usually with many parameters, pretrained on large-scale and diverse data to learn general-purpose representations or predictive capabilities that transfer across downstream tasks. After pretraining, it can be adapted through fine-tuning, instruction tuning, prompting, retrieval, tool use or other methods. The term usually implies broad reuse across applications, but definitions differ: some authors restrict it to models with substantial scale and wide task transfer, while others use it more loosely for any broadly pretrained base model. It is related to, but not identical with, large language models, multimodal models or frontier models.

keyTakeaway: A foundation model is best understood as a reusable starting point for many AI applications, not as a finished product or a guarantee of quality.

quickCheck.question: Which description best fits a foundation model?
options: A fixed rule-based system written for one exact workflow
A broadly pretrained model that can be adapted for many later tasks
Any AI system that produces human-like conversation
The most powerful model available anywhere at a given time
quickCheck.explanation: The key idea is broad pretraining plus later adaptation for multiple downstream uses. A rule-based system is different, a chatbot is just one possible application, and 'most powerful available' refers more to frontier model discussions than to the definition of foundation model.
